x.ASV: Why do the nations rage, And the peoples meditate a vain thing?
x.Darby: Why are the nations in tumultuous agitation, and [why] do the peoples meditate a vain thing?
x.KJV: Why do the heathen rage, and the people imagine a vain thing?
x.YLT: Why have nations tumultuously assembled? And do peoples meditate vanity?

nt: The proper understanding of the questions that make up this verse is provided in [verses 4](../002/004.md) and those that follow. They are not true questions; they are statements of mocking disbelief. If you would not use the question form for this purpose in your language, you could translate this as a statement or an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Nations are in turmoil and peoples are complaining uselessly.]

Here, **nations** represents either the people of the nations or the leaders of the nations. If **nations** could not be understood to **conspire**, you could use an equivalent expression from your language or state the meaning plainly. However, it is best to not narrow the meaning to leaders yet, as the psalm will do that in the next verse. Alternate translation: [people from other nations]

What the **nations** are conspiring and the **peoples** are plotting is not mentioned in this verse, but since it becomes clear from the next two verses, you do not need to explain its meaning further here.

x.ASV: The kings of the earth set themselves, And the rulers take counsel together, Against Jehovah, and against his anointed, saying,
x.Darby: The kings of the earth set themselves, and the princes plot together, against Jehovah and against his anointed:
x.KJV: The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the Lord, and against his anointed, saying,
x.YLT: Station themselves do kings of the earth, And princes have been united together, Against Jehovah, and against His Messiah:

nt: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. However, if it would be helpful to your readers, you could connect the phrases with a word other than **and** in order to show that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [The kings of the earth take their stand; indeed, the rulers conspire together]

x.ASV: Let us break their bonds asunder, And cast away their cords from us.
x.Darby: Let us break their bonds asunder, and cast away their cords from us!
x.KJV: Let us break their bands asunder, and cast away their cords from us.
x.YLT: `Let us draw off Their cords, And cast from us Their thick bands.'

nt: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could connect the phrases with a word other than **and** in order to show that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [Let us tear apart their bonds; truly, let us cast their cords away from us.]

The people of other nations speak of Yahweh and his anointed one’s rule over them as if it were **bonds** and **cords**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [We should free ourselves from their control; we should not let them rule over us any longer]

x.ASV: He that sitteth in the heavens will laugh: The Lord will have them in derision.
x.Darby: He that dwelleth in the heavens shall laugh, the Lord shall have them in derision.
x.KJV: He that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh: the Lord shall have them in derision.
x.YLT: He who is sitting in the heavens doth laugh, The Lord doth mock at them.

nt: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could connect the phrases with a word to show that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [He who sits in the heavens sneers; indeed, the Lord mocks them.]

The psalmist is referring specifically to God **sitting** on his throne, and he is using that action to represent God ruling. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [He who is enthroned] or [He who rules]

x.ASV: Then will he speak unto them in his wrath, And vex them in his sore displeasure:
x.Darby: Then will he speak to them in his anger, and in his fierce displeasure will he terrify them:
x.KJV: Then shall he speak unto them in his wrath, and vex them in his sore displeasure.
x.YLT: Then doth He speak unto them in His anger, And in His wrath He doth trouble them:

nt: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **anger** and **fury**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [when he is angry and … with how furious he is]

x.ASV: Yet I have set my king Upon my holy hill of Zion.
x.Darby: And I have anointed my king upon Zion, the hill of my holiness.
x.KJV: Yet have I set my king upon my holy hill of Zion.
x.YLT: `And I--I have anointed My King, Upon Zion--My holy hill.'

nt: This verse is a quotation of Yahweh (who is mentioned before this verse as the Lord who is sitting in the heavens). If the speaker would be unclear, you may want to introduce him as the UST does.

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I will cut** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize how significant it was that it was he and not someone else who was setting up this king on Zion. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [I alone have poured out]

Scholars debate the meaning of this verb. However, all the options lead either symbolically or literally to the idea that Yahweh has made his king the ruler on Zion. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have installed] or [I have placed]

x.ASV: I will tell of the decree: Jehovah said unto me, Thou art my son; This day have I begotten thee.
x.Darby: I will declare the decree: Jehovah hath said unto me, Thou art my Son; I this day have begotten thee.
x.KJV: I will declare the decree: the Lord hath said unto me, Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee.
x.YLT: I declare concerning a statute: Jehovah said unto me, `My Son Thou art, I to-day have brought thee forth.

nt: The person saying this is the king that Yahweh placed in Zion. This is a change of speaker from the previous verse, though both are unmarked in the original. You can include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [The king says he will describe a decree of Yahweh]

x.ASV: Ask of me, and I will give thee the nations for thine inheritance, And the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession.
x.Darby: Ask of me, and I will give thee nations for an inheritance, and for thy possession the ends of the earth:
x.KJV: Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession.
x.YLT: Ask of Me and I give nations--thy inheritance, And thy possession--the ends of earth.

nt: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **inheritance** and **possession**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [for you to inherit and … you shall possess]

Here, **the extremities of the earth** is referring to all of the world by naming its edges or limits. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the entire world]

x.ASV: Thou shalt break them with a rod of iron; Thou shalt dash them in pieces like a potter’s vessel.
x.Darby: Thou shalt break them with a sceptre of iron, as a potter's vessel thou shalt dash them in pieces.
x.KJV: Thou shalt break them with a rod of iron; thou shalt dash them in pieces like a potter’s vessel.
x.YLT: Thou dost rule them with a sceptre of iron, As a vessel of a potter Thou dost crush them.'

nt: תְּ֭רֹעֵ⁠ם בְּ⁠שֵׁ֣בֶט בַּרְזֶ֑ל כִּ⁠כְלִ֖י יוֹצֵ֣ר תְּנַפְּצֵֽ⁠ם

Here the king is speaking of his own power and anger as if it was an **iron rod** and of nations as if they were a **jar of a potter**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning another way. Alternate translation: [Your power is like an iron rod, which will shatter the nations, which are like mere clay pots.]

Using a simile in the second clause is a way to intensify the statement in biblical poetry. Use a method in your language’s poetic forms to intensify the second clause if possible. Alternate translation: [more than that, you will smash them to pieces like a jar of a potter]

A **potter** is a person who makes clay pots and jars. These are fragile and can be broken easily. If your readers would not be familiar with this, you could use the name of something similar in your area or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [like a clay jar]

x.ASV: Now therefore be wise, O ye kings: Be instructed, ye judges of the earth.
x.Darby: And now, O kings, be ye wise, be admonished, ye judges of the earth.
x.KJV: Be wise now therefore, O ye kings: be instructed, ye judges of the earth.
x.YLT: And now, O kings, act wisely, Be instructed, O judges of earth,

nt: If your language does not use this passive form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [listen to this warning]

x.ASV: Serve Jehovah with fear, And rejoice with trembling.
x.Darby: Serve Jehovah with fear, and rejoice with trembling.
x.KJV: Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice with trembling.
x.YLT: Serve ye Jehovah with fear, And rejoice with trembling.

nt: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **fear** and **rejoice**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [fearfully, and joyfully tremble]

x.ASV: Kiss the son, lest he be angry, and ye perish in the way, For his wrath will soon be kindled. Blessed are all they that take refuge in him.
x.Darby: Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and ye perish in the way, though his anger burn but a little. Blessed are all who have their trust in him.
x.KJV: Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and ye perish from the way, when his wrath is kindled but a little. Blessed are all they that put their trust in him.
x.YLT: Kiss the Chosen One, lest He be angry, And ye lose the way, When His anger burneth but a little, O the happiness of all trusting in Him!

nt: To **kiss the son** is a symbolic action showing loyalty and pledged obedience. If this would not be clear to your readers, you can explain the significance of this action in the text or in a footnote. People would show their king that they were loyal to him by kissing him, perhaps on the feet. Alternate translation: [Show the son that you are truly loyal to him] or [Bow down humbly before his son]

The implication is that the **son** will kill you if you are not loyal to him. You can include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and he kill you in the way]

The anger of the **son** is spoken of as if it were a fire that **burns**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when he suddenly becomes very angry]

The protection that submitting to the **son** provides is spoken of as if the son himself were a safe place or **refuge** within which people could be protected. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Everyone who asks the king to protect them is happy]

The psalmist is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of joy or blessing. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Oh, how happy are]
